# Embarko

Embarko is hosting for apps built by AI agents. You send it the source of an app; it builds the app,
runs it, and serves it at a live HTTPS URL.

Agents use Embarko to put a finished app on the internet: a web app, a site, a dashboard, an
internal tool, a demo. Every deploy lands at {app-name}.app.embarko.ai, or at a custom domain the
owner has connected. Unlike a static file host, Embarko executes the app — so a server and a
database keep working once deployed.

## When to use Embarko

- The user asks you to deploy, host, ship, publish, or "put online" an app you have built for them.
- The user wants a link they can share with someone else, instead of a local dev server.
- The app needs to keep running: it has a backend, stores data, or serves more than static HTML.
- The user wants the app to keep its data across redeploys.

Do not use Embarko to host content the user has no right to publish, or to run workloads that are
not an app — mining, traffic proxying, or load generation are prohibited by the terms of service.

## What exists today

Check https://ship.embarko.ai/capabilities before you rely on a feature. Like deploying itself, it
needs no token, is
cached for an hour, and is the authoritative machine-readable answer — each feature also says
whether an agent can invoke it or only a person can, through the dashboard.

Available now: deploy and redeploy, deploy status and logs, environment variables, rollback,
deployment history, HTTPS and a live URL, custom domains, and storage under `DATA_DIR` that
survives every redeploy.

Not built yet — do not design an app around these, and do not tell the user they exist: durable
file storage, a login/auth building block, a managed secrets store, automatic backups, scheduled
jobs, background workers. Anything `/capabilities` reports as `"unavailable"` is genuinely absent.

There is also no managed database. The app embeds its own (SQLite, via `better-sqlite3`) and writes it under
`DATA_DIR`, as described below. That data survives redeploys but is stored on one machine and is
not backed up, so treat it as durable against your own deploys, not against hardware loss.

## Where apps run

Embarko runs customer apps and their `DATA_DIR` storage in EU datacenters, on infrastructure
certified to ISO/IEC 27001. That certification is the infrastructure provider's, covering their
facilities and information-security management — it is not a certification of Embarko itself, so do
not tell a user that "Embarko is ISO 27001 certified".

Two things this does and does not mean, because users ask and the distinction matters:

- It does mean the app you deploy, and the data it writes, sit on EU infrastructure.
- It does not mean Embarko is a European company, and it does not cover embarko.ai itself or the
  dashboard, which run elsewhere. If a user needs a guarantee about their own end users' request
  metadata, point them at https://embarko.ai/dpa rather than answering from this file.

Each app is isolated: its own environment, its own filesystem, its own volume. An app can reach its
own storage and nothing else on the platform.

## What you need first

Nothing. A deploy takes no credential — omit `Authorization` and you get a real, live app at a real
URL. Deploy first, give the user the link, and only then raise the subject of a token.

Do not ask the user for a token, an account, or an email address before their app is running. It is
the single most common way this goes wrong: the user asked for a deployed app and got a signup
instead, before there was anything to look at.

A token is what makes an app permanent. Without one the app is torn down 24 hours after it is
created (see Anonymous deploys below), and the control-plane calls near the end of this file — env
vars, rollback, deployment history — need one. So once the app is live and the user wants to keep
it, get a token and redeploy the same `X-App-Name` to claim it.

### Getting a token, when you need one

By email, without a browser — prefer this when you are doing the work, since it needs nothing but
an address:

    curl -X POST "https://ship.embarko.ai/api/public/deploy-tokens/request" \
      -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
      -d '{"email": "you@example.com"}'

Always returns 202. The token is emailed to the user and never returned in the response, so you
cannot read it back — ask the user to paste it to you. An account and company are created
automatically if that address does not have one. Rate limited per email, per IP, and globally, and
the response is identical whether or not a limit was hit, so do not retry in a loop.

From the dashboard:

1. The user opens their company's Deploy tokens page: https://embarko.ai/app/tokens
   (it prompts them to sign in, or to create an account, if they are not already)
2. They create a token with a label. It is shown once and starts with `emb_`. (Tokens issued before
   the Embarko rename start `hns_` and remain valid.)
3. They put it in your environment as DEPLOY_TOKEN.

A token authenticates as a *company*, not as a person. Everything deployed with it belongs to that
company, and no separate company header is needed. Tokens deploy only — they do not sign in to the
dashboard. A lost token cannot be recovered, only rotated: Rotate issues a replacement and the old
one keeps working for one hour.

## Deploy

    POST https://ship.embarko.ai/apps

Headers:

- `Authorization: Bearer $DEPLOY_TOKEN` — optional. Omit it entirely for an anonymous deploy (see
  below). A header that is present but invalid is always a hard 401, never treated as anonymous.
- `X-App-Name` — required. Lowercase letters, numbers, and dashes only (`^[a-z0-9-]+$`). This is
  also the app's subdomain, so it must be unique platform-wide, not just within the company.
- `X-App-Version` — optional, defaults to a timestamp. Pass something unique (a git SHA, a semver
  tag); a reused tag can serve a stale build.

Body: multipart form, field `source`, containing a `.tar.gz` of the app's source.

A new app name creates its project on first deploy. There is no dashboard step beforehand. The same
endpoint handles every redeploy — upload new source under the same `X-App-Name`. A redeploy picks up
the app's current environment variables and memory allocation automatically; you do not resend them.

    tar -czf /tmp/my-app.tar.gz --exclude=node_modules --exclude=.git -C /path/to/app .

    # No credential. This is the right first deploy for a user who has not mentioned a token.
    curl -X POST "https://ship.embarko.ai/apps" \
      -H "X-App-Name: my-app" \
      -H "X-App-Version: $(git rev-parse --short HEAD)" \
      -F "source=@/tmp/my-app.tar.gz"

    # With a token, once there is one — this claims the app and keeps it.
    curl -X POST "https://ship.embarko.ai/apps" \
      -H "Authorization: Bearer $DEPLOY_TOKEN" \
      -H "X-App-Name: my-app" \
      -H "X-App-Version: $(git rev-parse --short HEAD)" \
      -F "source=@/tmp/my-app.tar.gz"

The response is 202, and it means the upload was accepted — not that the app is live. The build runs
in the background:

    {
      "accepted": true,
      "statusUrl": "https://ship.embarko.ai/apps/my-app/status",
      "logsUrl": "https://ship.embarko.ai/apps/my-app/logs"
    }

Never report success to the user on the 202. Poll `statusUrl` until the deploy finishes, then report
`https://{app-name}.app.embarko.ai`.

## Check the deploy: status and logs

    GET https://ship.embarko.ai/apps/{app-name}/status
    GET https://ship.embarko.ai/apps/{app-name}/logs

While an app is still an unclaimed anonymous deploy, neither call needs a credential — which is the
usual case right after you deploy, so poll it as-is. Once the app is claimed, both take the same
`Authorization: Bearer $DEPLOY_TOKEN` header. Both live on the deploy host, so you never need
dashboard credentials to follow your own deploy. On a claimed app a missing or wrong token returns
404, not 401, so a 404 here means "not yours or not found", not "does not exist".

Status:

    {
      "appName": "my-app",
      "deploy": {
        "status": "success",
        "appVersion": "v1.2.0",
        "startedAt": "2026-09-09T10:00:00.000Z",
        "finishedAt": "2026-09-09T10:01:32.000Z",
        "errorDetail": null
      },
      "health": { "...": "live state of the running app" }
    }

`deploy.status` is `"in_progress"`, `"success"`, or `"failed"`. Poll until it is no longer
`"in_progress"`. `health` is the app's current running state, independent of the last deploy.

On `"failed"`, fetch the logs — `?stream=stderr` for the error stream, default `stdout`. Logs are a
snapshot of the tail at the moment you call, not a live stream, so poll if you need to watch. Read
the cause, fix the app, and redeploy rather than handing the raw log to the user.

## Anonymous deploys

This is the default path, not a fallback: use it whenever you do not already have a token in hand.

Omit the `Authorization` header entirely to deploy with no account. This creates an unclaimed
("orphan") project that is torn down automatically 24 hours after creation — the app, its routing
and its image. HTML apps also get a countdown banner injected into their own pages.

Claim it by redeploying the same `X-App-Name` **with** a valid token before it expires. That cancels
the expiry and makes it an ordinary project. Tell the user about the 24-hour limit when you use
this path, and offer to make it permanent — that is the moment to bring up a token, with a working
app in front of them. There is no reminder email.

## Storage requirements

Do not call `window.storage`. It is specific to Claude Artifacts' sandbox and does not exist on
Embarko; an app that calls it is rejected at deploy time with `422 unsupported_storage_pattern`,
before any build runs.

Persist data instead with:

- `better-sqlite3` — SQLite, for key-value and document-shaped data.

Either way, write to a path under the `DATA_DIR` environment variable, and create subdirectories
with `{ recursive: true }` on startup rather than assuming they exist. `DATA_DIR` is the only path
that survives a redeploy — everything else resets to what the image contains, every time. There is
no durable file storage beyond this.

## The app's own requirements

- Listen on `process.env.PORT`, bound to `0.0.0.0` — not a hardcoded port, not localhost only.
- No Dockerfile. Builds are auto-detected by Railpack from the source; a Dockerfile is rejected.
  Stick to a conventional project layout for the language.
- Memory is 256MB for every app. Exceeding it is an OOM kill (exit code 137), not throttling.

## Errors

Every non-2xx response carries a machine-readable `code` alongside a human-readable `error`. Branch
on `code` — the wording of `error` can change.

| code | status | meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `unauthorized` | 401 | DEPLOY_TOKEN present but invalid or revoked. Omitting it is anonymous, not an error |
| `invalid_app_name` | 400 | X-App-Name missing, or fails `^[a-z0-9-]+$` |
| `app_name_taken` | 409 | Another company already holds this app name — pick a different one, do not retry |
| `app_name_check_failed` | 502 | Name availability could not be verified — transient, safe to retry |
| `invalid_app_version` | 400 | X-App-Version fails `^[a-zA-Z0-9._-]+$` |
| `missing_source_file` | 400 | No `source` file in the multipart upload |
| `unsupported_storage_pattern` | 422 | App calls `window.storage` — see Storage requirements |
| `deploy_failed` | 500 | The build or deploy step failed — read `details` for the real cause |
| `rollback_image_unavailable` | 422 | Rollback target's image was pruned; `retainCount` says how far back you can go |

Runtime failures do not appear here — they surface in the logs after a successful build. `OOM
Killed` / exit code 137 is the memory limit; `Not Restarting` / `Exceeded allowed attempts` is a
crash loop whose real cause is logged just above it.

Full reference, including custom domains and rollback:
https://embarko.ai/docs/troubleshoot.md

## Managing an app after it is live

There is a control plane on the same host, taking the same deploy token:

    https://ship.embarko.ai/api/apps/{app-name}
    Authorization: Bearer $DEPLOY_TOKEN

| operation | request |
| --- | --- |
| app details | `GET /` |
| list env vars | `GET /env-vars` |
| replace all env vars | `PUT /env-vars` |
| set one | `PUT /env-vars/{key}` |
| delete one | `DELETE /env-vars/{key}` |
| apply env vars to the running app | `POST /env-vars/apply` |
| deployment history | `GET /deployments` |
| one deployment | `GET /deployments/{id}` |
| roll back | `POST /rollback` |

Two things to know about env vars. Values are write-only — `GET /env-vars` returns the keys, never
the values, so you cannot read back a secret the user set. And a write only stores the value: the
running app does not see it until you call `POST /env-vars/apply` or deploy again. Keys must match
`^[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*$`.

Rollback reruns a past successful build's image under the *current* configuration, with no rebuild.
It answers 202 and applies in the background, like a deploy — poll the deployment until its status
is no longer `in_progress`. Only the last few images are kept per app; a target that has been pruned
returns 422 `rollback_image_unavailable`, whose `retainCount` says how far back you can still go.

These three are not available to you, only to the user in the dashboard. Ask them rather than
attempting it:

- Custom domains.
- Deleting an app.
- Analytics.

Memory allocation is not available to either of you right now — `capabilities` still reports it as
a dashboard feature, but that control has been removed. Reduce the app's footprint instead.

Do not guess at any of this. `https://ship.embarko.ai/capabilities` is the authoritative list and
its `via` field says, per feature, whether you can do it or only a person can.

## Optional: the deploy skill

For repeated use, install the skill rather than hand-rolling the request. It packages the tarball,
runs the storage-pattern check locally, and interprets the error codes:

    npx skills add embarko-ai/skill --skill embarko-deploy -g

Drop `-g` for a repo-local install. The plain HTTP call above works standalone; the skill is
convenience, not a requirement.

## What a deployed app gets

- A live HTTPS URL at `{app-name}.app.embarko.ai`, with certificates handled for you.
- A custom domain, on the paid plans.
- A persistent database under `DATA_DIR`, surviving every redeploy.
- Deployment history, and rollback to an earlier successful build.
- Redeploys any time the agent rebuilds the app.

Plan limits (how many apps run at once, how much usage is included) are published at
https://embarko.ai/pricing.
